spec.title: Policies, deadlines, defaults and break glass

item.title: Break glass: the owner's lever, never the scheduler's
Rows and codes this domain owns

spec.purpose: An escalation nobody answers by its deadline gets the default its policy row names, as a record first and a wake second, bounded per ticket. Break glass is routed and never decided: the owner grants one command once, on the page.

section.title: What the policies domain decides

node.title: A standing policy's default is a policy.applied record naming the row and the escalation it answers, written before the wake it implies, bounded by a limit per ticket counted from the log, and never defined for a break glass

section.text: In: the policies table, the records since the boundary, the clock. Out: for each escalation past its deadline, one record job and one prompt job after it.

section.title: The policies table
section.text: A row: an id in the policy form, a match on kind, code and optional attempt, deadline seconds, the kinds that answer it, a limit per ticket, the decision it rests on, and a default with do, to and the answer text.
A row whose match is break.glass is refused at load with exit 3, at start and on reload alike: a table that covered it would let the line grant itself the one thing it must never grant itself.
Policy ids are unique or the table is refused.
The table reloads like the routes table: a bad file is kept out with one 500 note and the loaded one stays.

section.title: Open escalations
section.text: An escalation is a record a row covers: its kind and code match and its attempt matches when the row names one. It is open while no record of one of the row's answering kinds has landed on the same ticket with a later id.
The deadline is the record's at plus the row's deadline seconds, judged against the clock; a default can land up to one poll interval late.
The index of records by ticket since the boundary is kept in memory by intake and shared; policies never list the log themselves.
Only records after intake's boundary are judged, so a log of old escalations never wakes every seat that ever blocked.

section.title: Applying a default
section.text: First a record job: policy.applied 200 on the ticket, with the policy id, the escalation's id as the answer, the role woken as the addressee, and the default text in the note after the words default and the policy id.

Then a prompt job after it: record, the printed id, playbook, the role's playbook path, to the seat the row's to names. Source means the escalation's own seat and role; a role name means that role's seat on the ticket.
The prompt is confirmed like every wake; a seat that does not pick up its default is a dead wake with a note, where the bash watch wrote one 500 and moved on.
A target with no seat name or role is one 500 note naming the policy and the escalation; the record stands so a re-seated seat finds its answer in the log.

section.title: Limits and the handled set
section.text: Defaults already applied to a ticket by a row are the policy.applied records on that ticket naming that policy, counted from the log; past the row's limit the escalation waits for a person, which is what the second blocked row does.
An escalation is handled when a policy.applied record answers its id, or when a job with its apply key exists in the store; no separate latch file, so a pruned log resets the count and nothing else.
Two escalations of one ticket and one row judged in one tick count against the limit together.

section.title: Break glass: the owner's lever, never the scheduler's
section.text: Only the owner authorises, on the page; one action per answer; the action is one plain command; the role comes back on the follow-up record or the ttl. The scheduler changes none of this: it routes the records and runs the seat script.
The 300 request goes to the interface agent as a decision line; the card on the page is the interface agent's.

The 200 runs the break-glass verb for the record's seat with the record id. The seat script reads the owner's answer from the page and refuses with exit 3 and its own 423 when a check fails; exit 3 is handled for this verb.
A 423 wakes the monitor with the record.
100 in effect, 201 the command finished, 204 the role settings restored: seen, receipted, nothing to do.
The scheduler never reads the page, never writes a 200, never has a policy for a break glass, and never runs the granted command: the seat does, under its own hook.
The restore sweep stays a periodic housekeeping job on the health domain's schedule, through the sweep verb, as the glass watcher pane runs it today.

section.title: Keys this domain reads
section.key: Role files for the reverse lookup and the seat names.
The playbook path on the wake line.

section.title: Rows and codes this domain owns
section.owns-route: notify the owner through the interface agent, line decision.
run the seat script's break glass for the record's seat.
wake the monitor with the record.
none: the default was recorded; the wake that follows it is the policy domain's own job.
section.owns-code: A break glass is over: the role's own settings are back and verified.
A request refused at the gate, with the failing key; never retried and never defaulted: a rejection waits for a new request.

example.text: A worker's blocked 423 sits thirty minutes with no ticket.cut or work.started after it; the scheduler writes policy.applied 200 naming the row and the 423, then wakes the worker with that record's id.

A break.glass 200 lands; the scheduler runs the seat script with the record id; the script finds no owner answer on the page, writes its 423 and exits 3; the job is done with exit 3 kept and the monitor is woken by the 423.
A policy row that defaults an unanswered break.glass 300 to granted after an hour.
example.why: The owner grants every break glass by hand, once.

example.text: Waking the seat with the default text typed into its pane and no record.
example.why: The board, the flow and the next seat read the log; a default taken in a prompt leaves no trace.
